aos.name: Unit 3 · Financial accounting for a trading business

topics.title: Double entry and the General Journal
points: Every transaction has at least one debit and one credit of equal value; the accounting equation always balances.
Debit increases: assets, expenses, drawings. Credit increases: liabilities, owner’s capital, revenue.
Special journals (Cash Receipts, Cash Payments, Sales, Purchases) are posted to ledger accounts; the General Journal records everything else, with a narration.
Ledger accounts (T-accounts) are balanced at the end of the period; a Trial Balance lists all balances and total debits should equal total credits.
A Trial Balance that balances can still hide errors: omission, reversal, wrong account, or the same mistake on both sides.
GST Clearing: credit for GST on sales, debit for GST on purchases.
topics.explain: Explain why a Trial Balance that balances does not prove the records are correct.

qs.q: Give the double entry for a credit sale of $1 100 including GST.
qs.a: Dr Accounts Receivable 1 100; Cr Sales 1 000; Cr GST Clearing 100 (plus Dr Cost of Sales and Cr Inventory at cost under a perpetual system)

qs.q: Which account normally has a credit balance?
Give the General Journal entry for the owner taking $200 of inventory (at cost) for private use.
qs.e: Narration: owner’s drawings of inventory, memo 12.

qs.q: Paying $500 to a creditor affects the equation by…

topics.title: Inventory and cost of sales
points: Perpetual inventory: inventory cards updated with every purchase, sale and return; Cost of Sales recorded at each sale.
Cost methods: identified cost or FIFO. Costs include purchase price, freight in and customs, but not GST.
Inventory is reported at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV); a write-down is an expense.
Stocktake differences: inventory loss (expense) or gain (revenue), recorded by General Journal.
Inventory management: avoid stock-outs and overstocking; watch Inventory Turnover; consider obsolete or slow-moving stock.
topics.explain: Explain why inventory must be written down to net realisable value.

qs.q: Freight paid to bring inventory into the store is…
o: part of the cost of inventory

qs.q: Stock costing $900 can only be sold for $700 less $50 selling costs. What is the write-down?
Which method assumes the oldest stock is sold first?

topics.title: Reports and cash flows
points: Income Statement: Revenue, Less Cost of Sales, Gross Profit, Less Inventory loss / Add gain, Add Other revenue, Less Other expenses (selling, administrative, finance), Net Profit.
Balance Sheet: current and non-current assets and liabilities; owner’s equity = capital + net profit − drawings.
Cash Flow Statement: operating, investing, financing activities. A reconciliation explains why Net Profit differs from net operating cash flow.
Differences come from accruals and prepayments, depreciation, credit transactions and GST timing.
Profit is not cash: a profitable business can still run short of cash.
topics.explain: Explain three reasons Net Profit might be higher than Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities.

qs.q: Depreciation expense of $2 000 in the reconciliation is…
qs.e: It reduced profit but used no cash.

qs.q: Buying a delivery van for cash is which activity?
Net Profit is $10 000 but Accounts Receivable rose by $3 000. Effect on operating cash?
qs.a: Cash from operations is $3 000 lower than profit, because some sales have not been collected.

aos.name: Unit 4 AoS 1 · Recording, reporting and balance day adjustments

topics.title: Balance day adjustments
points: Accrued expense (owed, not yet paid): Dr Expense, Cr Accrued Expense (current liability).
Prepaid expense (paid in advance): an asset; at balance day, Dr Expense, Cr Prepaid Expense for the part used.
Accrued revenue (earned, not yet received): Dr Accrued Revenue (current asset), Cr Revenue.
Unearned revenue (received in advance): a current liability until it is earned.
Depreciation: Dr Depreciation expense, Cr Accumulated Depreciation. Bad debts: Dr Bad Debts, Cr Accounts Receivable.
Adjustments apply the accrual basis and period assumptions, so revenue and expenses match the period.
topics.explain: Explain why wages owed at 30 June must be recorded even though no cash has been paid.

qs.q: Wages of $800 are owed at 30 June. Give the balance day adjustment.
Rent paid in advance at balance day is reported as…
Fees received from a client for work not yet done are…
A debtor owing $400 goes bankrupt. Record the write-off.
qs.a: Dr Bad Debts 400; Cr Accounts Receivable 400

topics.title: Closing the ledger
points: Revenue and expense accounts are closed to the Profit and Loss Summary at the end of the period.
The Profit and Loss Summary balance (net profit or loss) is closed to Capital.
Drawings are closed directly to Capital.
Asset, liability and capital accounts are balanced and carried forward to the next period.
Closing entries keep each period separate (period assumption).
topics.explain: Explain why revenue and expense accounts start each year at zero.

qs.q: Give the closing entry for Sales of $50 000.
qs.a: Dr Sales 50 000; Cr Profit and Loss Summary 50 000

qs.q: Drawings are closed to…
Which account is not closed at year end?

topics.title: Budgets
points: Budgeted Cash Flow Statement: expected cash receipts and payments (no depreciation; includes GST and loan principal).
Budgeted Income Statement: expected revenue and expenses on an accrual basis.
Budgeted Balance Sheet: expected financial position at the end of the period.
Cash collected from AR = opening AR + credit sales (incl. GST) − closing AR.
Variance reports compare actual with budget: favourable or unfavourable, then explain causes and suggest action.
topics.explain: Explain why depreciation appears in the budgeted Income Statement but not the budgeted Cash Flow Statement.

qs.q: Opening AR $5 000, credit sales $22 000 (incl. GST), closing AR $6 000. Find cash received from customers.
Which item appears in a budgeted Cash Flow Statement but not a budgeted Income Statement?
Budgeted sales $80 000, actual $74 000. State the variance.

topics.title: Performance analysis and decisions
points: Profitability: ROI, ROA, Asset Turnover, NPM, GPM, Expense ratio (expense ÷ sales × 100).
Liquidity: WCR, QAR, Cash Flow Cover; efficiency of collection and payment: AR, AP and Inventory Turnover.
Stability: Debt Ratio and Interest Cover where taught.
Strategies: raise prices or mark-up, cut costs, promote, chase debtors, offer discounts, reduce stock levels, refinance debt.
Consider ethical, social and environmental factors as well as financial ones.
Always use the figures: state the trend, explain it, then advise.
topics.explain: Advise an owner whose AR Turnover rose from 30 to 50 days on 30-day credit terms.

qs.q: Offering a discount for early payment mainly aims to…
o: speed up cash collection from customers

qs.q: Net Profit $12 000, average capital $80 000. Find the Return on Owner’s Investment.
A Quick Asset Ratio of 0.6 : 1 suggests…
o: the business may struggle to pay immediate debts
